name: Memory-safety vulnerability identification and exploit construction
theory_paragraphs: A running program lives in a \term{process address space} divided into regions: the \term{code} region (the machine instructions, normally read-only), \term{global data}, the \term{heap} (memory reserved at run time by \texttt{malloc} and released by \texttt{free}), and the \term{stack}. The stack exists because every function call must remember where to continue when the function finishes: just before jumping into a called function, the CPU pushes the \term{return address} --- the address of the next instruction of the caller --- onto the stack. Each call also creates a \term{stack frame} holding the function's local variables and the \term{saved frame pointer} (a bookmark to the caller's frame). On the exam's usual model the \imp{stack grows toward lower addresses}, so a frame contains, from high to low addresses: function arguments, saved return address, saved frame pointer, then local variables. Two facts do all the work in these problems: (i) an array write \texttt{a[i]} moves toward \emph{higher} addresses as \texttt{i} grows, so writing past the end of a local array walks \emph{upward} through the frame toward the saved return address; (ii) pointers are 4 or 8 bytes, and x86 stores multi-byte values \term{little-endian}, meaning the least significant byte comes first: the address \texttt{0x4012b0} must be embedded in a payload as the byte sequence $\texttt{b0}\,\texttt{12}\,\texttt{40}\,\texttt{00}$.

A \term{memory-safety violation} is any read or write outside the region an object legitimately occupies. The recurring bug classes, and \emph{why} each one is wrong: \begin{tightitem} \item \term{Buffer overflow}: more bytes written than the destination holds. Caused by functions that never check the destination size: \texttt{gets} (reads a whole line, no limit), \texttt{strcpy}/\texttt{strcat} (copy until a NUL byte in the \emph{source}), \texttt{sprintf}, \texttt{scanf}/\texttt{fscanf} with \%s, and \texttt{memcpy(dst, src, len)} when $\texttt{len} > \texttt{sizeof(dst)}$. \item \term{Buffer over-read}: more bytes read than the object holds. The exam favourite: \texttt{strcat(buffer, input)} on an \emph{uninitialized} \texttt{buffer} --- \texttt{strcat} must first find the terminating NUL of \texttt{buffer}, but an uninitialized local contains garbage left by earlier frames, so the scan runs out of bounds and may leak adjacent memory (the Heartbleed bug was an over-read). \item \term{Use-after-free / dangling pointer}: a pointer used after \texttt{free}; the allocator may hand the same bytes to a new object, so attacker data is reinterpreted as the old object. \item \term{Type confusion}: a wrong cast reinterprets an object as another type. \item \term{Uninitialized memory} and \term{double free}: expose stale values or corrupt allocator metadata. \end{tightitem}

Why is a stack overflow so powerful? Because the CPU \emph{trusts} the saved return address blindly: the \texttt{return} instruction simply pops whatever bytes sit in that slot and jumps there. This gives three escalation levels, in increasing distance from the buffer. (i) \term{Adjacent-local overwrite}: the bytes just past the buffer belong to another local --- an authentication flag or a pointer --- so a few extra bytes change program logic without touching any control data. This is often the shortest attack and the one students forget: a canary never sees it. (ii) \term{Return-address hijack}: fill the buffer, the intervening locals and the saved frame pointer, then overwrite the saved return address; on \texttt{return} the CPU jumps to an address of the attacker's choice, for example an existing privileged function in the binary (\term{code reuse}; \term{return-oriented programming}, ROP, chains short existing instruction snippets called \term{gadgets}). (iii) \term{Shellcode injection}: the payload itself is machine code placed inside the overflowed buffer, and the return address is pointed back into the buffer. Shellcode must be \term{position-independent} (it runs correctly no matter what address it lands at, meaning it contains no hard-coded absolute addresses) and contain no NUL bytes if it travels through string functions; its goal is usually to invoke \texttt{execve}, the system call that replaces the current process with a chosen program such as \texttt{/bin/sh}. Injection requires \imp{an executable region and a known buffer address}.

Defenses, and --- this is what the exam actually tests --- precisely which attack each one \emph{misses}: \begin{tightitem} \item \term{Stack canary}: a random per-execution value placed between the locals and the saved frame pointer, checked just before \texttt{return}. A linear overflow cannot reach the return address without also overwriting the canary, so return-address hijacks are detected --- but \imp{a canary does not protect adjacent locals}, because a flag or pointer hijack happens before the check, and it guards the stack only, never the heap. \item \term{NX / W$\oplus$X} (no page both writable and executable): the stack and heap can no longer be executed, so injected shellcode dies --- but \imp{jumps to existing code survive} (ret2func; \term{ret2libc}, jumping to existing library functions such as \texttt{system()} instead of injected code; ROP), because those reuse bytes that are legitimately executable. \item \term{ASLR} (address-space layout randomization): randomizes base addresses. \imp{Stack-only ASLR preserves relative offsets} inside the stack and leaves code and heap addresses fixed, so a payload living on the heap, or a jump to a fixed code address, is unaffected. \item \term{Guard pages}: unmapped pages placed between regions that trap a linear overflow crossing the boundary; useless for an overflow that stays inside one frame. \item \term{Safe APIs and languages}: bounded copies (\texttt{fgets}, \texttt{strncpy}, \texttt{snprintf}) and explicit length checks remove the overflow itself; memory-safe languages remove the whole bug class. \end{tightitem}

Putting it together, every exam instance is the same three-act play. Act 1: find the lines where attacker-controlled bytes or lengths reach a fixed-size object --- and say \emph{which region} (stack or heap) each line endangers. Act 2: draw the layout in address order, measure the distance in bytes from the buffer to the chosen target, and write the payload as \imp{filler plus a little-endian address}. Act 3: for each named defense, do not ask ``is it a good defense'' but \imp{which memory region and which attack step it actually covers} --- that single question answers every canary/NX/ASLR/guard-page sub-question in this unit.
theory_cheatsheet: Frame layout (high $\rightarrow$ low): args, saved return address, saved frame pointer, locals; array writes go toward higher addresses, so overflows walk up toward the return address.
Padding to reach the return address $=$ buffer size $+$ bytes of intervening locals $+$ saved frame-pointer size. Payload $=$ filler $+$ target address in little-endian byte order.
\imp{Canary is checked only at return}: it never protects flags or pointers overwritten earlier in the frame, and never guards the heap.
NX/W$\oplus$X stops injected shellcode only; jumping to existing functions (ret2func, ret2libc, ROP) still works.
Stack-only ASLR hides stack addresses but \imp{preserves relative offsets} and does not move heap or code: heap payloads and fixed code targets survive.
\texttt{strcat} on an uninitialized buffer over-reads while hunting for the NUL byte; \texttt{memcpy} copies NUL bytes, string functions stop at them.
Fix pattern: bounded copy (\texttt{fgets}/\texttt{strncpy}/\texttt{snprintf}), explicit check $\texttt{len} \leq \texttt{sizeof(dst)}$, initialize buffers, prefer a memory-safe language.
identify_givens: A short C program (5--15 lines) with attacker-controlled input (a \texttt{char*} from argv/stdin plus possibly an attacker-chosen length), containing a fixed-size stack buffer and/or a heap allocation, and one or more unsafe calls: \texttt{gets}, \texttt{strcpy}, \texttt{strcat}, \texttt{sprintf}, \texttt{fscanf} \%s, or \texttt{memcpy} with an unchecked length. The problem often states the stack layout (grows down, order of locals, pointer size), mentions an existing target function at a known address or a secret/flag variable, and later sub-questions name defenses: stack canary, NX/W$\oplus$X, ASLR (stack base only vs full), guard pages.
identify_target: Identify the vulnerable lines and say why they are unsafe; construct a concrete attacker input that corrupts an adjacent local (flag/pointer), overwrites the saved return address to reach an existing function or injected shellcode (stating assumptions about executability and known addresses); then judge for each named defense whether it stops each attack and why, and propose a working countermeasure for any attack that survives.
strategy_name: Trace the overflow into the layout, then match each defense to the attack it misses

algorithm.detail: Scan for unbounded copies: \begin{tightitem} \item \texttt{gets}, \texttt{strcpy}, \texttt{strcat}, \texttt{sprintf}, \texttt{scanf}/\texttt{fscanf} \%s into a fixed buffer; \item \texttt{memcpy(dst, src, len)} with attacker-controlled $\texttt{len} > \texttt{sizeof(dst)}$; \item \texttt{strcat}/\texttt{strlen} on an uninitialized buffer (out-of-bounds read hunting for the NUL byte); \item pointer used after \texttt{free}, type-confusing casts, double free. \end{tightitem} State for each flagged line \emph{which} memory region (stack/heap/global) it endangers.

Write down the relevant region in address order using the stated conventions. Stack growing down: arguments, saved return address, saved frame pointer, then locals; record exact byte counts and the pointer size (4 or 8 bytes). Confirm which local sits adjacent to the overflowable buffer --- \imp{the layout decides which attack is shortest}. For heap bugs, note the allocation size and what object or metadata follows it.

Choose the weakest point: \begin{tightitem} \item an adjacent local: flip an auth flag to nonzero, or retarget a data pointer so a later \texttt{strcmp} or write uses attacker bytes; \item the saved return address, reached with $\texttt{buffer\_size} + \texttt{intervening\_locals} + \texttt{sizeof(saved\_fp)}$ bytes of padding; \item heap metadata or an adjacent heap object; \item a dangling pointer via use-after-free. \end{tightitem}

Express the payload as a byte-count formula plus concrete bytes. Flag flip: $\texttt{sizeof(buffer)} + 1$ bytes with a nonzero last byte lands in the adjacent \texttt{int}. Return hijack: padding up to the saved return address, then the target address (e.g. the existing privileged function) in \term{little-endian} order, plus optional extra words that the target will read as arguments. Pointer retargeting: filler, then the address of the attacker's own buffer.

State the required assumption explicitly (\imp{executable stack or heap}). Place machine code (shellcode: position-independent, NUL-free, sets up \texttt{execve}) inside the attacker-controlled buffer, overwrite the saved return address with the buffer's own address, and on return the CPU jumps into the shellcode. State what you assume about knowing the buffer address (debugger, leaked pointer, no ASLR).

algorithm.action: Match each defense to the attack it misses
algorithm.detail: Evaluate per defense, per attack: \begin{tightitem} \item stack canary (checked just before return): stops return-address overwrites, not adjacent-local corruption --- the hijack happens before the check; \item NX/W$\oplus$X: stops injected shellcode, not jumps to existing functions (ret2func/ROP); \item stack-base ASLR: hides stack addresses but preserves relative offsets and leaves heap/code addresses known --- a heap-resident payload or fixed code target survives; full ASLR also randomizes libraries; \item guard pages: trap linear overflows crossing a region boundary, useless within a single frame. \end{tightitem}

Replace unsafe calls with bounded APIs (\texttt{fgets}, \texttt{strncpy}, \texttt{strncat}, \texttt{snprintf}, or an explicit check $\texttt{len} \leq \texttt{sizeof(dst)}$), initialize buffers before use, free once and NULL the pointer, add a canary for return-address protection, and prefer a memory-safe language. For each fix, name the original attack it kills.

variations.name: Adjacent local overwrite instead of return address
variations.detail: Some sittings ask for an input (other than the correct password) that makes the program take a privileged path; the shortest answer overflows a small buffer by one nonzero byte into an adjacent \texttt{int} auth flag --- no return address needed. Trap: students only write the classic return-address smash and miss the shorter attack. A second variant retargets an adjacent \texttt{char*} so a later \texttt{strcmp(input, input)} trivially succeeds. Canaries stop neither, because the corruption happens before the canary check at return.

variations.name: Heap overflow mixed with uninitialized-buffer over-read
variations.detail: One reexam mixes \texttt{memcpy(tmp, input, len)} with $\texttt{len} > 32$ (heap overflow), a stack overflow, and \texttt{strcat} on an uninitialized \texttt{buffer[32]} (out-of-bounds read while searching for the NUL byte). Adapt by analyzing each line separately and naming the affected region per line. Trap: forgetting that an uninitialized buffer has no NUL terminator, so the over-read occurs before any copying.

variations.name: Defense quiz with scope reversal (stack ASLR vs heap payload)
variations.detail: Per-defense verdicts with a scope trap: randomizing only the stack base defeats a jump to a stack-resident shellcode buffer but \emph{not} the same payload placed on the heap at a known address --- stack randomization does not move the heap. Guard pages do not stop an intra-frame stack overflow but can detect a heap overflow past a buffer if placed between heap regions. For every defense, ask \imp{which memory region it actually protects}.

variations.name: Shellcode vs return-to-existing-function
variations.detail: Some sittings provide an existing target function so no injection is needed (jump to its known address); others demand injected code, which requires stating the executable-stack assumption and a known buffer address. Notation traps: the pointer size (4 vs 8 bytes) changes the padding length, and little-endian byte order matters when writing the address into the input.

walkthrough_problem: A packet-processing daemon contains an existing function \texttt{spawn\_console} at address \texttt{0x4011c8} that opens a privileged console. The code below is not memory safe (\texttt{packet} and \texttt{plen} are attacker-controlled, pointers are 8 bytes; the chunk returned by \texttt{malloc} stores \texttt{user} at offset 0 and the 8-byte function pointer \texttt{on\_done} at offset 16; the stack grows down, and within the frame of \texttt{dispatch} the buffer \texttt{cmd} is the lowest local, with the saved frame pointer and the saved return address directly above it): \texttt{struct session \{ char user[16]; void (*on\_done)(void); \}; void enroll(char *packet, unsigned plen) \{ struct session *s = malloc(sizeof(struct session)); s->on\_done = log\_close; memcpy(s->user, packet, plen); /* Line A */ s->on\_done(); /* Line B */ \} void dispatch(char *packet, unsigned plen) \{ char cmd[24]; memcpy(cmd, packet, plen); /* Line C */ exec\_cmd(cmd); /* Line D: unknown commands are ignored */ \}} (a) Identify the vulnerable line(s) and explain why they are unsafe. (b) Give a value of \texttt{plen} and an input to \texttt{enroll} that makes the daemon execute \texttt{spawn\_console}, without touching any return address. (c) Give a value of \texttt{plen} and an input to \texttt{dispatch} that redirects execution to \texttt{spawn\_console} when \texttt{dispatch} returns, stating your byte layout and endianness. (d) Explain how the attacker could instead run injected code via \texttt{dispatch}, stating the required assumptions. (e) Does a stack canary stop attack (b)? Attack (c)? (f) Does NX (W$\oplus$X) stop attack (d)? (g) Which of attacks (b), (c), (d) survive if only the stack base is randomized? (h) Propose a countermeasure that fixes the root cause.

walkthrough_steps.work: Line A, \texttt{memcpy(s->user, packet, plen)}: \texttt{s->user} is a 16-byte heap field, but \texttt{plen} is attacker-controlled and never checked, so choosing $\texttt{plen} > 16$ is a heap overflow --- and because \texttt{on\_done} sits at offset 16 of the same chunk, the overflow can reach a \emph{function pointer}. Line C, \texttt{memcpy(cmd, packet, plen)}: same pattern into a 24-byte \emph{stack} buffer, so it is a stack overflow. Line B is not itself a memory error, but it is the escalation point: it calls whatever pointer the overflow installed --- always check \emph{who consumes} the corrupted data. Beginner trap: thinking \texttt{memcpy} is safe because it takes a length; the length only helps if someone validates it. Note also that unlike \texttt{strcpy}, \texttt{memcpy} copies NUL bytes, so addresses containing \texttt{0x00} survive delivery intact.

Heap chunk of \texttt{s}: \texttt{user} occupies offsets 0--15, \texttt{on\_done} occupies offsets 16--23. Stack frame of \texttt{dispatch}, from high to low addresses: saved return address (8 bytes), saved frame pointer (8 bytes), then \texttt{cmd[24]} as the lowest local. Why this ordering matters: array writes from \texttt{memcpy(cmd, ...)} move toward \emph{higher} addresses, so overflowing \texttt{cmd} hits the saved frame pointer first and the saved return address second. Without this picture you cannot compute any padding length --- draw it every single time.

For (b), the cheapest target is \texttt{on\_done}: it lives exactly $16$ bytes past the start of \texttt{user}, the hijack fires at the indirect call in Line B, and \emph{no return address is involved at all} --- which is exactly what sub-question (b) demands. For (c), the target is the saved return address, which sits $24 + 8 = 32$ bytes past the start of \texttt{cmd} (buffer plus saved frame pointer). Choosing the target \emph{before} writing bytes is what keeps the arithmetic clean.

Set $\texttt{plen} = 24$ and send 16 filler bytes (\texttt{A}$\times 16$) followed by the 8-byte little-endian encoding of \texttt{0x4011c8}, i.e. $\texttt{c8}\,\texttt{11}\,\texttt{40}\,\texttt{00}\,\texttt{00}\,\texttt{00}\,\texttt{00}\,\texttt{00}$. The first 16 bytes exactly fill \texttt{user}; the next 8 overwrite \texttt{on\_done}; Line B then executes \texttt{spawn\_console()}. Two beginner mistakes to avoid: writing the address in big-endian order (x86 is little-endian --- least significant byte first), and worrying about the five NUL bytes in the address --- \texttt{memcpy} does not stop at \texttt{0x00}, so they are delivered fine (a string-based copy would truncate this payload).

Set $\texttt{plen} = 40$ and send 32 filler bytes followed by the same little-endian \texttt{0x4011c8}. The 32 filler bytes cover \texttt{cmd} (24 bytes) and the saved frame pointer (8 bytes); the final 8 bytes land exactly on the saved return address. When \texttt{dispatch} returns, the CPU pops our address and jumps to \texttt{spawn\_console}. Sanity check a beginner should always do: total payload $= 24 + 8 + 8 = 40 = \texttt{plen}$ --- the counts must be consistent or the marker will subtract points.

walkthrough_steps.step_ref: Step 6: Injection variant (d) and the defense verdicts
walkthrough_steps.work: (d) Assume the stack is executable and the address of \texttt{cmd} is known (no ASLR, or a leaked pointer): put position-independent machine code at the start of \texttt{packet}, pad to 32 bytes, append the little-endian address of \texttt{cmd}, set \texttt{plen} to the total; on return, execution enters the injected code. Verdicts, each justified by \emph{what the defense covers}: (e) the canary sits between \texttt{cmd} and the saved frame pointer and is checked just before return, so it stops (c) --- but \emph{not} (b), because \texttt{s} lives on the heap where no canary exists, and the hijack fires at the indirect call before any return. (f) NX/W$\oplus$X makes the stack non-executable, so it stops (d); it does nothing against (b) and (c), which jump to \emph{existing} code. (g) Stack-base-only ASLR defeats (d) as stated (the address of \texttt{cmd} becomes unknown) but neither (b) nor (c): stack randomization moves neither the heap chunk nor the fixed code address \texttt{0x4011c8}, and relative offsets inside the stack are preserved.

(h) Validate the length before each copy: \texttt{if (plen > sizeof s->user) return;} before Line A and \texttt{if (plen > sizeof cmd) return;} before Line C (or clamp \texttt{plen} to the destination size, or use bounded APIs). Removing both overflows kills all three attacks at the root --- this is always the strongest answer to a ``propose a countermeasure'' sub-question, with defenses like \term{control-flow integrity} (a mechanism that restricts indirect calls to a pre-approved set of legitimate targets, so a hijacked function pointer cannot jump to attacker-chosen code) on the indirect call, or guard pages between heap chunks, mentioned only as additional layers.

exam_questions.source: Exam HT2018 (2019-01-14), Part II Problem 3 (Buffer overflow)
exam_questions.problem: (1) Describe the content of the stack while \texttt{check\_pwd} is executed. (2) Write an input for the program (different than ``12345'') that makes the program execute \texttt{do\_something} and explain why this happens. (3) Explain how this problem can be fixed. \texttt{int check\_pwd(char *pwd) \{ int result; char input[10]; result = 0; gets(input); if (strcmp(input, pwd) == 0) result = 1; return result; \} void main() \{ int auth = check\_pwd(``12345''); if (auth) do\_something(); \}}

solution_steps.work: The only dangerous line is \texttt{gets(input)}: \texttt{gets} reads a whole line of input with \emph{no length limit} into the 10-byte stack array \texttt{input} --- the classic stack buffer overflow. \texttt{strcmp} only reads and is not the bug. (Official solution: answers to part (1) assume a 32-bit layout with 4-byte pointers.)

solution_steps.step_ref: Step 2: Draw the memory layout (answer to part 1)
solution_steps.work: Official stack content while \texttt{check\_pwd} executes, from high to low addresses: \begin{tightitem} \item saved return address, \item saved frame pointer, \item \texttt{pwd} (a 4-byte \emph{pointer} to the string ``12345'' --- not a buffer of chars), \item \texttt{result} (4-byte \texttt{int}), \item \texttt{input[10]} (10 bytes). \end{tightitem} Since \texttt{gets} writes toward higher addresses, overflowing \texttt{input} reaches \texttt{result} first (after 10 bytes), then \texttt{pwd} (after $10+4$), then the saved frame pointer and the return address.

Three targets at increasing distance from \texttt{input}: the flag \texttt{result} at byte offset $10$; the pointer \texttt{pwd} at offset $10 + 4 = 14$; the saved return address at offset $10 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 22$. The official solution gives one attack per target --- part (2) accepts any input that makes \texttt{do\_something} run, so the shortest (the flag flip) is the best exam answer.

solution_steps.step_ref: Step 4: Construct the concrete inputs (answer to part 2)
solution_steps.work: Official attacks: \begin{tightitem} \item (a) Adjacent-local overwrite: provide $11$ bytes of text whose last byte is different from NUL. Ten bytes fill \texttt{input}; the 11th nonzero byte lands in \texttt{result}, making it nonzero, so \texttt{check\_pwd} returns a true value and \texttt{main} calls \texttt{do\_something}. \item (b) Pointer retargeting: provide $10 + 4$ bytes, the last 4 being the address of \texttt{input} itself. This overwrites \texttt{pwd} to point at \texttt{input}, so \texttt{strcmp(input, input) == 0} and \texttt{result} becomes 1 --- the official remark is that \texttt{pwd} is a pointer, not a buffer. \item (c) Return-address hijack: provide $10 + 4 + 4 + 4$ filler bytes followed by the address of \texttt{do\_something} (little-endian), so the return from \texttt{check\_pwd} jumps straight into \texttt{do\_something}. \end{tightitem}

solution_steps.step_ref: Step 6--7: Match defenses and fix (answer to part 3)
solution_steps.work: Official fix: use a safe API (bounded input such as \texttt{fgets} with an explicit size) --- this removes the overflow itself and therefore kills all three attacks; alternatively a stack canary, which protects against the return-address overwrite (attack (c)) because the canary sits between the locals and the saved frame pointer and is checked just before return. Note that a canary alone would \emph{not} stop attack (a) or (b): those corrupt \texttt{result} and \texttt{pwd} before any canary check happens.

exam_questions.answer: An 11-byte input whose last byte is nonzero overflows \texttt{input[10]} into \texttt{result}, so \texttt{auth} becomes true and \texttt{do\_something} executes; fix with a bounded input API (or a stack canary against the return-address variant).

exam_questions.problem: The following program is not memory safe; \texttt{input} and \texttt{len} are controlled by an attacker. \texttt{void process(char *input, size\_t len) \{ char buffer[32]; char *tmp = malloc(32); if (tmp == NULL) return; memcpy(tmp, input, len); // Line A free(tmp); // Line B strcat(buffer, input); // Line C printf(``\%s\textbackslash n'', buffer); // Line D return; \}} (6a) Identify the lines that have a problem and explain why they are not secure. (6b) Explain how an attacker can exploit the vulnerabilities to gain control of the program's execution: which memory region is corrupted, what part of the state is overwritten, how execution is redirected. (6c) Explain how the attacker can inject and execute new code, including your assumptions about the binary and memory layout. (6d) Can the attack in 6c be countered by randomizing the base address of the stack? (6e) Can the attack in 6b be countered by guard pages? (6f) Where the proposed countermeasures fail, propose and motivate a different one.

solution_steps.work: Official solution: Line A --- \texttt{tmp} points to 32 heap bytes but \texttt{len} is attacker-controlled; if $\texttt{len} > 32$ this is a \term{heap buffer overflow}. Line C has \emph{two} issues: \texttt{buffer} is uninitialized, so \texttt{strcat} may read out of bounds while searching for the first NUL terminator (an over-read); and \texttt{strcat} performs no bounds checking, so appending attacker-controlled \texttt{input} can cause a \term{stack buffer overflow} of \texttt{buffer[32]}. Lines B and D are not memory errors.

solution_steps.step_ref: Step 3--4: Pick the target and hijack control (answer to 6b)
solution_steps.work: Official solution: the most direct path is the stack overflow at Line C. The attacker supplies \texttt{input} such that \texttt{strcat(buffer, input)} writes beyond the 32-byte buffer (region corrupted: the \emph{stack}). The overflow overwrites the saved frame pointer and the saved return address of \texttt{process}'s frame (state overwritten). The attacker writes an address of their choosing, e.g. an existing function, over the saved return address; when \texttt{process} returns, the CPU jumps to that attacker-chosen address (redirection).

solution_steps.step_ref: Step 5: Build the code-injection variant (answer to 6c)
solution_steps.work: Official solution: assuming the stack is executable, the attacker places the injected binary code inside \texttt{input} and uses attack (b) to overwrite the saved return address with the address of the injected code (i.e. pointing the return back into the attacker-controlled data). Stated assumptions: executable stack (no NX) and knowledge of the target buffer's address (no ASLR).

solution_steps.step_ref: Step 6: Match defenses to what they miss (answers to 6d and 6e)
solution_steps.work: Official solution: (6d) Yes for the attack in (c) as stated, since the attacker will no longer know the address of \texttt{buffer}. \emph{However}, the payload is also copied into \texttt{tmp} on the heap by Line A, so the attacker can instead point the return address to \texttt{tmp} (assuming the heap address is known), because \imp{stack randomization does not affect the heap}. (6e) No: guard pages do not help because the overflow exploited in (b) is on the stack inside a single frame; guard pages could only help if placed between heap data structures to detect the overflow of \texttt{tmp} at Line A.

solution_steps.step_ref: Step 7: Propose the real fix (answer to 6f)
solution_steps.work: Official solution: a simple solution is a stack canary (detects the return-address overwrite before \texttt{process} returns). A better solution fixes the root causes: initialize \texttt{buffer}, check that \texttt{len} is less than 32 before Line A, and limit \texttt{strcat} to write at most 32 bytes (e.g. a bounded concatenation).

exam_questions.answer: Line A is a heap overflow (len > 32) and Line C is an uninitialized-buffer over-read plus a stack overflow; overwriting the saved return address (or pointing it at injected code on an executable stack) hijacks execution; stack ASLR fails because the payload also lives in tmp on the heap, guard pages do not help an intra-frame stack overflow; fix with a stack canary plus length checks, buffer initialization and bounded strcat.

exam_questions.problem: The program below receives an argument and prints it (\texttt{./main hello} prints \texttt{hello}); \texttt{Pwd123456} is a secret that must not be leaked, and \texttt{strcmp(input, secret)} returns 0 only if the two strings are equal. \texttt{void printInput(char *input) \{ char buffer[50]; char secret[20] = ``Pwd123456''; if (strcmp(input, secret) == 0) print(secret); else printf(input); strcpy(buffer, input); \} int main(int argc, char *argv[]) \{ if (argc != 2) return 1; printInput(argv[1]); return 0; \}} The attacker controls the input argument. (7a) Identify the lines that have a problem and explain why. (7b) Explain a mechanism to force the program to execute arbitrary code: what should the argument be, and what assumptions about the binary and memory layout do you make? (7c) Explain a mechanism to leak the password without injecting new code and without providing \texttt{Pwd123456} as input. (7d) Can the attack in 7b be countered by randomizing the base address of the stack? (7e) Can the attack in 7c be countered by randomizing the base address of the stack? (7f) For whichever attack survives, propose and motivate a countermeasure.

solution_steps.work: Official solution: the \texttt{strcpy(buffer, input)} line can overflow \texttt{buffer}, because it copies until the NUL in \emph{input} and will write more than 50 bytes whenever the input string is longer than 49 characters. Note the overflow happens \emph{after} the \texttt{strcmp}/\texttt{printf} logic, so it corrupts the frame regardless of which branch was taken.

Official assumption (stated in the sample solution): in the stack we have, from low to high addresses, \texttt{secret}, \texttt{buffer}, return pointer; the architecture is 64-bit, so pointers are 8 bytes. Writes from \texttt{strcpy} go toward higher addresses, so overflowing \texttt{buffer} reaches the saved return pointer.

solution_steps.step_ref: Step 5: Inject and execute arbitrary code (answer to 7b)
solution_steps.work: Official solution: the input contains 50 bytes, then $<$address of return pointer $+ 8>$, then the binary code. \texttt{strcpy} overflows the stack variables and overwrites the return pointer with the address immediately after the return pointer; the overflow additionally writes the binary code into that spot. Therefore, when the function returns it jumps to the address just above the return pointer on the stack --- straight into the injected code. Assumptions: executable stack and knowledge of the stack addresses.

solution_steps.step_ref: Step 3--4: Leak the secret without injection (answer to 7c)
solution_steps.work: Official solution: the input contains 50 bytes, then $<$address of \texttt{printf(secret)}$>$. \texttt{strcpy} overflows the stack variables and overwrites the return pointer with the address of the code that calls \texttt{printf(secret)}; when the function returns it jumps there and the password is printed. No new code is injected --- the attack reuses code already in the binary, which is exactly why NX would not help either.

solution_steps.step_ref: Step 6: Match the defense to what it misses (answers to 7d and 7e)
solution_steps.work: Official solution: (7d) Attack (b) \emph{is} countered by stack base randomization, since it prevents the attacker from knowing the address of \texttt{buffer} and therefore the address where the binary code has been injected --- the value to write into the return pointer becomes unknown. (7e) Attack (c) is \emph{not} countered: randomizing the stack base affects neither the distance between \texttt{buffer} and the return pointer nor the position of the \texttt{printf(secret)} code, both of which are all the attack needs.

solution_steps.step_ref: Step 7: Propose the countermeasure for the survivor (answer to 7f)
solution_steps.work: Official solution: a stack canary, placed between \texttt{buffer} and the return pointer. Assuming the attacker does not know the value of the random canary, the overflow overwrites the canary; when the function returns, the program checks the canary, detects that it has been altered, and aborts instead of jumping to the attacker's address.

exam_questions.answer: 7b: input = 50 bytes + (address of return pointer + 8) + binary code, so return jumps into the injected code (stopped by stack ASLR); 7c: input = 50 bytes + address of printf(secret) leaks the password via code reuse (ASLR fails; a stack canary stops it).
